subject: science
title: KS3 / Year 7-9 Science - Physics: Electricity Reading
subtitle: Reading questions on circuits, measurements, practical data and safety.
description: A reading pack for KS3 electricity. Passages cover circuit basics, measuring current and voltage, resistance investigations, series and parallel circuits, and electrical safety.

data.sourcePassage: Electricity transfers energy using moving electric charge. In a simple school circuit, charge can flow only if there is a complete conducting loop. The circuit also needs an energy source, such as a cell or a battery, to provide a voltage. A closed switch completes the loop, so current can flow and a lamp can light. An open switch creates a gap, so current cannot flow all the way round. Components such as lamps, buzzers and motors are loads because they transfer electrical energy into useful forms such as light, sound or movement.

questions.question: What two things does a simple circuit need for current to flow?
questions.modelAnswer: It needs a complete conducting loop and an energy source such as a cell or battery.

questions.question: What does a closed switch do?
questions.modelAnswer: A closed switch completes the circuit.

questions.question: Why will a lamp not light if the switch is open?
questions.modelAnswer: An open switch creates a gap, so charge cannot flow all the way round the circuit.

questions.question: Explain why a motor is described as a load.
questions.modelAnswer: A motor is a load because it transfers electrical energy into movement or kinetic energy.

data.sourcePassage: Current is the rate of flow of electric charge and is measured in amperes. An ammeter measures current and must be connected in series, so the current being measured flows through it. Voltage, also called potential difference, is the energy transferred per coulomb of charge between two points. A voltmeter measures voltage and is connected in parallel across a component or supply. This is because it compares the energy per unit charge at two different points. A common mistake is to say that voltage flows. Current flows, but voltage is a difference between two points.

questions.question: What is current?
questions.modelAnswer: Current is the rate of flow of electric charge.

questions.question: How should a voltmeter be connected?
questions.modelAnswer: A voltmeter should be connected in parallel across the component.

questions.question: Why is an ammeter connected in series?
questions.modelAnswer: It must be in series so the current being measured flows through the ammeter as part of the same loop.

questions.question: Correct the misconception that voltage flows around a circuit.
questions.modelAnswer: Current flows around a circuit. Voltage is a difference in energy per unit charge between two points.

data.sourcePassage: A series circuit has one loop. The current is the same through every component, and the supply voltage is shared between components. Adding more identical lamps in series increases the total resistance, so the current decreases and the lamps are dimmer. If one component breaks, the whole circuit stops. A parallel circuit has more than one branch. Current splits at junctions and the branch currents add together when they rejoin. Each branch receives the full supply voltage, so lamps in parallel can be about as bright as one lamp. Homes use parallel circuits because lights and appliances need to work independently.

questions.question: Which circuit type has only one loop?
questions.modelAnswer: A series circuit has only one loop.

questions.question: What happens to current at a junction in a parallel circuit?
questions.modelAnswer: The current splits between the branches and rejoins later.

questions.question: Why do identical lamps become dimmer when more are added in series?
questions.modelAnswer: The total resistance increases, the current decreases, and the supply voltage is shared between more components.

questions.question: Explain why parallel circuits are more suitable for home lighting.
questions.modelAnswer: Each branch receives the full supply voltage and can work independently, so one failed lamp does not turn off every other lamp.

data.sourcePassage: In a practical investigation, a student can change the voltage across a fixed resistor and measure the current through it. Voltage is the independent variable because it is changed deliberately. Current is the dependent variable because it is measured. Control variables include using the same resistor, the same circuit setup and similar temperature where possible. If the graph of current against voltage is a straight line through the origin, current is directly proportional to voltage. Repeated readings help check repeatability. An anomalous result might be caused by a loose connection, a misread meter or a recording error.

questions.question: What is the independent variable in the investigation described?
questions.modelAnswer: The voltage across the resistor is the independent variable.

questions.question: Which variable is measured in this investigation?
questions.modelAnswer: The current is measured.

questions.question: What does a straight line through the origin on a current-voltage graph show?
questions.modelAnswer: It shows that current is directly proportional to voltage.

questions.question: Give two possible causes of an anomalous current reading.
questions.modelAnswer: Possible causes include a loose connection, a misread meter or a recording error.

data.sourcePassage: Mains electricity in the UK is about 230 V, much higher than low-voltage school circuits. It can be dangerous because a large current through the body can be fatal. Plastic or rubber insulation covers conductors in cables because these materials have very high resistance and reduce the chance of current flowing into people. Water near mains electricity is dangerous because tap water can conduct, and wet skin has lower resistance than dry skin. A fuse contains a thin wire that melts if the current is too high. This breaks the circuit and helps protect wiring and appliances from overheating.

questions.question: What is the approximate voltage of UK mains electricity?
questions.modelAnswer: UK mains electricity is about 230 V.

questions.question: Why is plastic used around copper wires?
options: It is an insulator that reduces shock risk
questions.modelAnswer: Plastic is an insulator that reduces shock risk.

questions.question: Explain why water near mains electricity is dangerous.
questions.modelAnswer: Tap water can conduct electricity and wet skin has lower resistance, so a larger current may pass through the body.

questions.question: Explain how a fuse reduces the chance of overheating.
questions.modelAnswer: If current is too high, the fuse wire heats up and melts, breaking the circuit so current stops flowing.
